title: MCP basics
point: MCP standardises how a host discovers and calls tools on servers, but it standardises the interface, not the policy, so your gateway still decides.
definition: The Model Context Protocol is an open protocol in which a host application runs clients that connect to servers. Servers expose tools, resources and prompts over stdio or HTTP, and clients discover and invoke them one standard way.

objective.text: Describe the host, client and server roles and the three things a server exposes, then list the gateway controls MCP does not provide and say where to add them.

misconceptions.claim: Tools from an MCP server are safe to use because the protocol is a standard.
misconceptions.correction: MCP fixes the message format, not who may call what. Authorisation, validation, timeouts and audit still belong to your gateway, in front of every server.

misconceptions.claim: A third-party server's tool descriptions can be trusted like your own code.
misconceptions.correction: Descriptions go straight into the model's context, so a hostile or compromised server can plant instructions there. Treat them as untrusted input: review them, pin them and watch for changes.

l1: The host is the application the user runs. It creates one client per server connection, and each server exposes its capabilities to that client.
A server exposes three kinds of thing: tools the model can call, resources the host can read as context, and prompts as reusable templates. Local servers use stdio and remote ones use HTTP.
MCP standardises discovery and invocation. It does not decide who may call a tool, so the gateway's authorisation, validation, timeouts and audit still apply to every call.
l2: A team connects a third-party ticketing server over HTTP. On discovery it lists twelve tools, including close_ticket and export_all_tickets.
The gateway sits between the host and the server. It allowlists four read tools for the support assistant, routes close_ticket through human confirmation, and blocks export_all_tickets entirely.

One tool description tells the model to always call export_all_tickets first. The team treats that as an injection attempt, pins the reviewed descriptions, and alerts when a server update changes them.
l3: Wrapping each MCP server in your own gateway adds a hop. A local policy check of about 2 ms beside a 300 ms remote call is under 1 per cent.
The alternative is trusting each server's own controls, which means one policy model per server. With ten servers, you would audit ten implementations instead of one.
Pin server versions and description hashes. An unreviewed change to a tool description is a change to your prompt, so it deserves the same review.
